newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank urges deficit cuts across Europe. [corrected 13:15 gmt]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank urges deficit cuts across Europe. [corrected 13:15 gmt]

text.p: The Bundesbank on Wednesday (Corrects from Thursday) urged Bonn and other European governments to renew efforts to cut their budget deficits, and warned that although German growth prospects were good, the jobs market would remain tight.
In its 1996 annual report the German central bank said that budget deficits in most European countries remained too high, adding this also placed a restriction on growth in the private sector.

Noting that European countries "with the exception of Germany" had made progress in reducing their budget deficits last year, the central bank nonetheless hit out at attempts by some countries to effect only temporary improvements.

"'Balance sheet cosmetics' clearly do not help in the task of consolidation," the central bank said. "They neither create new fiscal policy scope nor strengthen the competitiveness of the private sector," it said.
Sustainability would be essential for those countries entering monetary union, it added without naming the countries that may qualify only cosmetically.
Countries which wish to join European monetary union at the planned start date in 1999 must reach key economic targets this year in order to qualify for entry.

Most countries are facing serious problems in trimming their budget deficits back to a target level of three percent of gross domestic product. Germany, which notched up a 3.8 percent deficit in 1996, plans to cut this to 2.9 percent in 1997.

In Brussels, the European Commission on Wednesday painted a rosy picture of the prospets for the single currency, forecasting that oly Italy and Greece were currently missing the deficit target needed to qualify.
In its report, the German central bank warned that Bonn should make extra efforts to rein in its deficit, as unforeseen events could otherwise endanger the achievement of its budgetary goal.

Prospects for this year's budget already looked less rosy than had been the case last autumn, given that last year's tax receipts came in lower than expected and the recent rise in unemployment, the Bundesbank said.
"It can also not be ruled out that further unexpected burdens on the budget may arise in the course of the year, whether on the income side or on particular types of expenditure," it added.

"In view of this position efforts are needed to achieve further savings," it said, adding that the reduction of the deficit was not only desirable with a view to Germany's qualification for the single currency under the EU's Maastricht treaty.

German economic growth was likely to gain pace after a pause in growth in the winter months, but the impact on the jobs market, where record unemployment has been placing a strain on Bonn's budgets, would only be limited, the bank said.

"The conditions for this (a pick-up in the pace of growth) seem to be generally extremely favourable, although considerable structural problems remain which prevent a broader-based upswing," the report said.

But it added: "Even if a clear economic recovery in the course of the year should put an end to the downtrend in employment levels and replaces it with an uptrend it is not likely that a strong fall in unemployment will result."
Favourable factors for a resumption of growth included the normalisation of the exchange rate, low interest rates and recent moderate wage increases, the Bundesbank said.
While export trade was still expected to be the main growth motor, the Bundesbank expressed hope that this positive stimulus could this year also spread to domestic investment activity.

"If export business proves favourable in the long term, then the prospects increase on the demand side for this, taken together with the favourable supply conditions and the improvement in the tax framework which it is to be hoped will soon take effect, to ignite companies' investment interest."
An increase in investment activity would also help the construction sector, whose weakness at the turn of the year was largely responsible for the sluggishness of the economy.
From the inflation side, the price-conscious central bank said it continued to see no real danger.
